paragraphs: In sequential games between opposing teams, teammates may hold different private information. This makes coordinating a team computationally difficult and prevents its strategies from being represented directly on the usual game tree. Consequently, techniques that work well for large two-player zero-sum games cannot simply be applied to teams.

The paper introduces a team-public-information representation. A team becomes a single coordinator who sees only information shared by all teammates. Instead of knowing each player’s private situation, the coordinator prescribes an action for every possible private state. This produces a two-player tree with strategies that have a direct behavioral interpretation.

The authors prove that the representation preserves payoffs and develop ways to construct much smaller representations without losing information. It also offers greater flexibility for designing abstractions. These results create a route to using abstraction, no-regret learning, and subgame solving in team games. Experiments compare the techniques with existing methods on a standard testbed; the representational advance does not itself remove the stated computational hardness.
icml-2022-a-marriage-between-adversarial.tldr: A payoff-preserving representation turns adversarial team games into two-player trees, enabling established game-solving techniques.

paragraphs: Learning methods often use optimization procedures tailored to a particular model family. This paper proposes Random Hypothesis Subspace Sampling, or RHSS, as a shared alternative. It begins with a hypothesis class, randomly selects k candidate hypotheses, and learns a model from their span: the collection of their linear combinations.

Once those candidates are selected, learning reduces to a linear least-squares problem. The stated computational cost is O(n k²), where n is the number of training examples. The theoretical analysis studies how well the sampled subspace can approximate the desired solution, using metric entropy and random-matrix properties to derive performance guarantees.

The authors apply the framework to kernel, network, and tree models. In their experiments, performance converges efficiently as k increases, and RHSS outperforms the tested model-specific alternatives: random Fourier features, random vector functional links, and extra trees. The contribution is a common sampling-and-fitting approach across several model families, backed by approximation theory and empirical results, rather than a separate learning procedure for each family.
icml-2022-a-model-agnostic-randomized-le.tldr: RHSS learns combinations of randomly sampled hypotheses through least squares, providing one framework for kernel, network, and tree models.

paragraphs: The Approximate-Proximal Point family, called APROX, uses models of an optimization problem to guide stochastic updates. The abstract describes existing advantages over standard stochastic gradient methods, including robustness to step-size choices, adaptation to problem difficulty, and compatibility with minibatching. This paper develops an acceleration scheme for that family.

The authors provide convergence guarantees that apply after a finite amount of computation. Their bounds are order-optimal in the problem-dependent constants and show larger speedups from minibatching. This connects faster progress per optimization process with the ability to use batches of samples effectively, rather than treating those benefits as separate concerns.

A stronger result applies to interpolation problems whose objectives satisfy additional growth conditions: the accelerated method converges linearly over a wide range of step sizes. Matching lower bounds in this setting identify fundamental constants and establish the optimality of the APROX family. Empirical tests support the theoretical account of gains from accurate modeling, acceleration, and minibatching. The linear-rate claim specifically depends on the stated interpolation and growth assumptions.
icml-2022-accelerated-optimal-and-parall.tldr: An accelerated APROX method achieves optimal convergence bounds and stronger minibatching speedups, with linear convergence under additional conditions.

paragraphs: A change point is a moment when the behavior of an observed time series suddenly shifts. Detecting such moments matters for monitoring processes whose reliability or safety depends on recognizing changing conditions. The paper introduces ADAGA, a Gaussian-process approach intended to recognize different kinds of these changes.

Its central feature is adaptation to both the mean and the covariance structure of the process. A mean change concerns the level around which observations vary. A covariance change concerns how those variations relate across time. Accounting for both lets the method address changes that cannot be described solely as a rise or fall in the average signal.

ADAGA uses a heuristic developed from statistical hypothesis testing to support this detection process. The authors report extensive experiments spanning different classes of change points, finding significantly greater accuracy than the state-of-the-art alternatives they evaluate. These findings support the method’s versatility across the tested changes. The contribution combines a broader view of what can change in a temporal process with an empirically effective detection approach.
icml-2022-adaptive-gaussian-process-chan.tldr: ADAGA detects changes in both time-series averages and covariance structure, improving accuracy over evaluated alternatives.

paragraphs: This paper explores how a more detailed model of a biological neuron could support learning. The motivation is a gap between the brain’s efficient learning and the capabilities of many biological models built from simple, single-compartment neurons. The authors propose a multi-compartment model of a pyramidal neuron.

The model uses bursts of activity and separates inputs arriving through dendrites. Together, these mechanisms could plausibly support target-based learning: the network is given a suggested internal solution rather than having to derive that solution through error backpropagation and credit assignment. Here, the target is a pattern of bursts distributed across neurons and time.

The authors also show that the neuronal architecture supports hierarchical imitation learning. This organizes difficult decisions over long time horizons into simpler subtasks, linking the proposed cellular mechanisms to a broader learning structure. The result is a model connecting burst-based internal targets with coordinated behavior at multiple levels. Its biological relevance is framed as plausible support for this learning mechanism, rather than evidence that the brain necessarily implements it.
icml-2022-burst-dependent-plasticity-and.tldr: A multi-compartment neuron model uses burst patterns to support target-based learning and hierarchical decomposition of imitation tasks.

paragraphs: Vertical federated learning trains a model collaboratively when different parties hold different features of the data. Coordinating that training requires exchanging intermediate results, making communication an important cost. This paper introduces Compressed Vertical Federated Learning, or C-VFL, to reduce the amount of information sent during training.

The server and participating parties perform several local iterations and periodically share compressed intermediate results. The analysis examines how errors introduced by compression affect learning. For non-convex objectives, the authors prove a convergence rate of O(1/√T), provided compression error remains bounded throughout training. They also give convergence requirements for common techniques, including quantization and top-k sparsification.

Experiments show communication reductions exceeding 90% without a significant accuracy decrease relative to vertical federated learning without compression. This supports compression as a practical way to reduce coordination costs in the evaluated settings. The theoretical contribution explains when this saving remains compatible with convergence, tying the behavior of the training procedure to explicit control of compression error.
icml-2022-compressed-vfl-communication-e.tldr: C-VFL compresses exchanged training results, reducing communication by over 90% in experiments while providing convergence guarantees under bounded compression error.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether Invariant Graph Networks behave consistently as graphs sampled from a graphon approach their underlying continuous description. A graphon specifies the structure from which graphs are sampled. This convergence question differs from asking which functions a network can express or whether repeated layers blur node representations.

The authors first establish stability of linear layers for general order-k networks, using a new interpretation of equivariant layers. They build on this result to prove convergence in a setting where edge weights are available and error is measured for graphon inputs. Thus, the accessible form of graph information is central to the guarantee.

When only sampled binary adjacency matrices are available, convergence cannot be guaranteed for arbitrary IGNs. The authors recover convergence for a restricted class, IGN-small, after estimating edge probabilities. This class remains expressive enough to approximate spectral graph neural networks arbitrarily well. Experiments on several graphon models support the theoretical statements, showing how convergence depends on both the observation setting and the network class.
icml-2022-convergence-of-invariant-graph.tldr: IGN convergence depends on available graph information, with guarantees recovered for a restricted but expressive class after edge-probability estimation.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket idea concerns finding small, useful subnetworks inside much larger randomly initialized neural networks. Pruning removes parts of the larger network to identify these smaller structures. This offers a route toward compact models that can retain competitive performance on demanding learning tasks.

Although practical pruning uses many architectures, theoretical evidence for the existence of lottery tickets had largely concentrated on fully connected feedforward networks with ReLU activations. This paper broadens that theoretical scope to networks containing convolutional and residual layers. It also allows almost arbitrary activation functions, extending beyond one particular choice of nonlinearity.

The authors prove that architectures in this broader family can contain lottery tickets with high probability. This gives theoretical support to their possible presence in network types commonly used in practice. The claim concerns existence with a probabilistic qualification: it does not say that every randomly initialized network contains a suitable ticket. The contribution therefore expands where lottery-ticket reasoning can be justified, connecting a practical pruning idea with a wider class of mathematical guarantees.
icml-2022-convolutional-and-residual-net.tldr: The paper proves that convolutional and residual architectures with broadly varied activations can contain lottery tickets with high probability.

paragraphs: Recommenders can change the preferences they are trying to satisfy. A system optimizing engagement over a long horizon may therefore have an incentive to make users easier to please. This paper proposes considering those induced changes before deployment, alongside the behavior a recommender is expected to generate.

The approach learns a predictive user model from historical interactions. That model captures preference dynamics and estimates how users would respond to hypothetical recommendation policies. To evaluate those changes, the authors define a trust region of acceptable, or safe, shifts. One possible reference is how preferences would evolve without interference from the recommender.

In simulated experiments, the learned model effectively estimates preferences and their responses to new recommenders. Systems optimized to remain within the trust region can avoid manipulative behavior while still producing engagement. The contribution combines prediction with a criterion for judging influence: forecasting a preference shift alone does not establish whether it is desirable. The reported evidence concerns simulation and the chosen notion of acceptable change.
icml-2022-estimating-and-penalizing-indu.tldr: A learned preference-dynamics model and a trust region for acceptable changes help recommenders avoid manipulation in simulated experiments.

paragraphs: Minimizing average prediction error gives more influence to populations represented by more training examples. When demographic groups are unevenly represented, this can produce models biased against minority groups. The paper addresses this representation problem by changing the importance assigned to individual training samples.

Its method learns adaptive sample weights with the aim of balancing demographic groups. It emphasizes examples that are prone to prediction errors while improving the effective representation of minority groups. The authors derive a closed-form rule for assigning weights and an efficient algorithm with theoretical convergence guarantees. They also analyze the fairness properties of the resulting model.

Experiments cover both classification and regression. The method achieves performance comparable to or better than evaluated state-of-the-art approaches, while balancing fairness and accuracy. It also shows robustness to label noise across the tested benchmark datasets. The contribution is a way to make training respond to uneven representation and prediction difficulty together, supported by both mathematical analysis and empirical evaluation.
icml-2022-fairness-with-adaptive-weights.tldr: Adaptive sample weights address demographic under-representation while balancing fairness and predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes provide a posterior variance that can help estimate prediction error and risk. In safety-critical applications, however, error guarantees often assume that the kernel hyperparameters are known. The paper addresses the mismatch between that assumption and settings where those parameters must be inferred from data.

The method constructs a confidence region over hyperparameters and uses it to obtain a probabilistic upper bound on model error for a Gaussian process with arbitrary hyperparameters. It does not require pre-specified bounds on the hyperparameters. Instead, the relevant bounds are derived from data, incorporating uncertainty about parameter choices into the error assessment.

The authors also use the technique to derive performance guarantees for a class of learning-based control problems. Experiments report that the proposed bound performs significantly better than vanilla and fully Bayesian Gaussian-process alternatives. The contribution is an error-bounding framework that accounts for unknown kernel settings. Its safety relevance comes from a probabilistic guarantee on error, rather than an unconditional assurance that a learned model will always be correct.
icml-2022-gaussian-process-uniform-error.tldr: Data-derived confidence regions over unknown kernel hyperparameters yield robust probabilistic error bounds for Gaussian processes.

paragraphs: IGLUE addresses an evaluation gap that has kept much vision-and-language research centered on English. It combines existing datasets with newly created ones to evaluate models across 20 languages. Its tasks cover answering questions about images, retrieving across text and images, reasoning grounded in images, and judging grounded entailment.

The benchmark evaluates transfer both without target-task examples and through newly defined few-shot setups. This makes it possible to examine whether multilingual multimodal models transfer directly and whether a small amount of additional supervision helps. Its breadth also allows performance to be compared across different kinds of image-grounded language understanding.

In evaluations of available leading models, translating test inputs performs better than direct zero-shot transfer, while few-shot learning is difficult to exploit for many tasks. The amount of unlabeled pretraining text partly explains downstream performance; linguistic distance between source and target languages explains it only weakly. These findings identify practical weaknesses in the evaluated models and provide a shared benchmark for studying them.
icml-2022-iglue-a-benchmark-for-transfer.tldr: IGLUE evaluates multilingual vision-and-language transfer across 20 languages, revealing difficulties with direct zero-shot and few-shot transfer.

paragraphs: The paper studies cooperation when an autonomous agent does not know the reward function shared with its partner. The partner may also act suboptimally. The learning agent must therefore discover what the pair is trying to achieve while choosing behavior that helps them perform well together.

The problem is modeled as an episodic two-agent Markov decision process, with control over only the first agent. In the Stackelberg formulation, the second agent seeks to maximize expected utility in response to the first agent’s policy. This makes interaction informative: changing the controlled agent’s policy can change the situation to which the partner responds.

The authors analyze how those interactions reveal the joint reward function. They show efficient reward learning when the learning agent’s policies have a significant effect on the transition function, which governs how the environment evolves. This condition identifies a useful role for influence over the interaction. It is a sufficient setting for efficient learning, rather than a claim that every cooperative pairing permits fast reward discovery.
icml-2022-interactive-inverse-reinforcem.tldr: An agent can efficiently learn a shared reward through cooperation when its policies significantly influence the environment’s transitions.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms depend on a rule for deciding how different two examples are. This paper introduces DID, a pairwise dissimilarity measure designed to use the internal structure of data. Its defining property is invariance to diffeomorphisms: smooth, invertible changes in the way that structure is represented.

The construction represents each datum as a function. It then defines the comparison through an optimization problem in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, a mathematical setting for working with functions using kernels. The resulting measure has a closed-form expression, connecting its optimization-based definition to a direct mathematical form.

For practical computation, DID can be approximated efficiently using Nyström sampling. The authors prove properties supporting theoretical study and practical use, and report empirical experiments supporting the measure’s merits. The contribution brings together structural invariance, a function-based formulation, and an efficient approximation route. Its intended reach spans a wide range of data spaces, making it a proposed general comparison tool rather than a measure restricted to one stated application.
icml-2022-measuring-dissimilarity-with-d.tldr: DID compares data through a kernel-based construction that is invariant to smooth invertible transformations.

paragraphs: Autonomous exploration here means learning how to reach a collection of states, rather than optimizing one fixed goal. The relevant targets are L-controllable states: states that can be reached incrementally from an initial state within L steps in expectation. The agent seeks a near-optimal policy for each such goal.

The authors introduce Value-Aware Autonomous Exploration and establish stronger sample-complexity bounds than previous algorithms. They also prove the first lower bound for this exploration problem. A lower bound describes an unavoidable learning cost, making it possible to assess how closely an algorithm approaches the best worst-case performance.

Comparing the bounds shows that the algorithm is nearly minimax-optimal when the number of L-controllable states grows polynomially with L. The design rests on a connection to multi-goal stochastic shortest path, a new extension of the classical single-goal problem. This connection organizes exploration around learning routes to multiple destinations and provides a second problem formulation that may be useful independently of the proposed algorithm.
icml-2022-near-optimal-algorithms-for-au.tldr: Value-Aware Autonomous Exploration improves sample bounds and is nearly minimax-optimal under a polynomial growth condition on reachable states.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decision-making with limited resources. A learner wants high expected reward while respecting several resource budgets. The challenge includes both stochastic inputs and adversarially chosen inputs, as well as reward and resource-consumption functions that need not be convex.

The authors formulate learning over mixtures of strategies. In that space, they recover strong duality for a Lagrangian relaxation, allowing the reward objective and resource constraints to be handled through an equivalent optimization relationship. This provides the foundation for a framework with no-regret guarantees in both stochastic and adversarial settings.

For stochastic inputs, the framework matches earlier regret guarantees. For adversarial inputs, it achieves a constant competitive ratio when budgets grow at least linearly with the time horizon, improving on a prior ratio that depends on the number of constraints and the logarithm of the horizon. Two game-theoretic applications illustrate flexibility. The budget-growth condition matters specifically to the stated adversarial competitive guarantee, while the formulation also accommodates non-convex rewards and costs.
icml-2022-online-learning-with-knapsacks.tldr: A strategy-mixture framework handles resource-constrained online learning in stochastic and adversarial settings, with stronger adversarial guarantees under sufficient budget growth.

paragraphs: The accelerated proximal point method, also known as Catalyst, solves a convex optimization problem through a sequence of regularized subproblems. This is an elegant way to obtain strong convergence guarantees. However, requiring very accurate solutions to those subproblems introduces an extra logarithmic factor in the overall computational bounds.

RECAPP changes the criterion used to decide whether a subproblem has been solved accurately enough. Its relaxed error requirement removes the need for high-accuracy intermediate solutions. The significance is that the outer accelerated procedure can retain strong guarantees without paying for more precision than it needs at every stage.

The authors apply the method to finite-sum optimization and max-structured minimization. For finite sums, RECAPP matches the best known complexity, previously achieved through carefully specialized algorithms. For objectives formed by maximizing a function that is convex in the minimization variable and strongly concave in the maximization variable, it improves the previous Catalyst-based bound by a logarithmic factor. These results show the value of changing the subproblem accuracy requirement within a general reduction.
icml-2022-recapp-crafting-a-more-efficie.tldr: RECAPP relaxes intermediate accuracy requirements in accelerated proximal optimization, matching or improving leading complexity bounds.

paragraphs: In partially observed reinforcement learning, an agent must act without directly seeing the full state of its environment. This paper studies a class of these problems with linear structure, allowing both the hidden-state space and the observation space to be infinite. The aim is learning efficiency governed by structure rather than space size.

The proposed algorithm, OP-TENET, combines three ingredients. A finite-memory Bellman operator describes values recursively. An adversarial integral equation identifies and estimates that operator using a smoothed discriminator tailored to the linear structure. Finally, uncertainty in this estimation drives optimistic exploration of the environment.

The authors prove that OP-TENET reaches an ε-optimal policy within O(1/ε²) episodes. Its sample complexity depends polynomially on the intrinsic dimension of the linear structure and does not depend on the sizes of the observation or state spaces. This provides a theoretical bridge between partial observability and function approximation. The guarantee applies to the structured class studied, showing how suitable low-dimensional organization can make very large partially observed problems statistically manageable.
icml-2022-reinforcement-learning-from-pa.tldr: OP-TENET learns near-optimal policies in linearly structured partially observed environments with sample complexity independent of state and observation space sizes.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a student using a teacher model’s outputs, while label smoothing changes the targets used to train that teacher. Earlier findings disagreed about whether these techniques work well together. This paper investigates that disagreement to clarify when a label-smoothed teacher is useful.

The authors identify and analyze a phenomenon they call systematic diffusion. According to their analysis, it reduces the benefits of transferring knowledge from a teacher trained with label smoothing, making distillation at increased temperatures ineffective. Temperature is therefore central to resolving the conflicting conclusions: evaluating label smoothing without considering the transfer temperature can obscure the interaction.

The discovery is supported by large-scale experiments, analyses, and case studies covering image classification, neural machine translation, and compact student models across multiple datasets and teacher–student architectures. Based on those findings, the authors recommend combining a label-smoothed teacher with low-temperature transfer to obtain high-performing students. The practical conclusion concerns how the two techniques are configured together, rather than a universal instruction to always accept or reject label smoothing.
icml-2022-revisiting-label-smoothing-and.tldr: Systematic diffusion helps explain conflicting distillation results and motivates using label-smoothed teachers with low-temperature transfer.

paragraphs: Imitation learning can produce a policy that works in its training environment but fails badly when the environment’s dynamics change. Dynamics determine how actions affect what happens next. A learner trained in a single setting may therefore reproduce behavior that depends too heavily on that particular setting.

The paper proposes learning from multiple experts associated with sampled versions of the environment dynamics. This exposes the learner to expert behavior across different conditions. To combine those sources of guidance robustly, the method minimizes a risk expressed through the Jensen–Shannon divergence between the agent’s policy and each sampled expert’s policy.

Numerical results show significantly improved robustness to dynamics perturbations compared with conventional imitation-learning baselines. The approach makes variation part of the imitation problem itself, rather than relying on demonstrations from only one environment. The stated findings support its effectiveness across the evaluated perturbations, with multiple sampled experts providing the basis for learning behavior that is less tied to a single set of dynamics.
icml-2022-robust-imitation-learning-agai.tldr: Imitating multiple experts across sampled environment dynamics improves robustness to dynamics changes in numerical evaluations.

paragraphs: Gaussian-process optimization becomes expensive as its evaluation history grows, because standard posterior computation has cubic cost in the number of observations. This paper uses a reformulation showing that the main computational burden depends on the number of distinct evaluated points. Repeated evaluations can therefore be handled more efficiently.

The proposed strategy stays with a candidate for multiple evaluations and switches only when needed. Limiting switches limits the number of unique historical inputs, allowing the required posteriors to be computed exactly and cheaply through the reformulation. This is especially relevant when changing candidates has its own cost, such as switching chemicals or loading data and models.

The authors adapt GP-UCB and GP-EI using switching rules drawn from batched optimization. These variants preserve their theoretical no-regret guarantees while improving runtime, memory requirements, and support for parallel batch evaluation. The contribution links candidate selection with computational efficiency: deciding when to revisit an input affects not only information gathering but also the cost of maintaining the optimization model.
icml-2022-scaling-gaussian-process-optim.tldr: Repeating candidate evaluations reduces distinct GP inputs, enabling cheaper exact posteriors while preserving optimization guarantees.

paragraphs: Learning control directly from images is often unstable in off-policy reinforcement learning. Successful methods have consequently relied on combinations of specialized practices and auxiliary losses. This paper analyzes a source of instability in the interaction between temporal-difference learning, a convolutional image encoder, and rewards with small magnitude.

The authors call this combination a visual deadly triad. Their analysis connects it to unstable training and early convergence to degenerate solutions, a failure mode they name catastrophic self-overfitting. This diagnosis focuses attention on how the visual representation is updated during learning, rather than treating instability only as an overall performance problem.

The proposed method, A-LIX, adaptively regularizes the encoder’s gradients using a dual objective designed to prevent that failure. On DeepMind Control and Atari, it significantly outperforms the prior state of the art without data augmentation or auxiliary losses. The result links an identified training mechanism to a targeted intervention, with benchmark evidence supporting the effectiveness of controlling the encoder’s gradient behavior.
icml-2022-stabilizing-off-policy-deep-re.tldr: A-LIX stabilizes learning from pixels by adaptively regularizing encoder gradients, improving results on DeepMind Control and Atari.

paragraphs: The Contextual Graph Markov Model learns probabilistic graph representations without supervision, training one layer at a time. A practical difficulty is choosing the size of the hidden representation in each layer. Searching over those sizes can require extensive model selection, as it does for many deep graph networks.

The paper introduces iCGMM, a Bayesian nonparametric extension that adapts each layer’s complexity during training to better fit the data distribution. This reduces the need to choose representation sizes through a separate search. The authors also develop an approximate inference procedure intended to handle larger graph topologies more effectively.

Across eight graph-classification tasks, iCGMM matches or improves the original model’s performance while reducing the hyperparameter search space. It also performs comparably to most evaluated end-to-end supervised methods. Additional studies examine depth, hyperparameters, and compression of graph embeddings. Together, these results support adapting representation complexity within training as a useful alternative to extensively searching over fixed layer sizes.
icml-2022-the-infinite-contextual-graph-.tldr: iCGMM adapts graph-representation complexity during training, reducing model-selection demands while maintaining or improving evaluated performance.

paragraphs: An extractive rationale highlights input text to explain a language model’s prediction. A useful rationale should reflect the model’s actual behavior, make sense to people, and preserve task performance. These goals are distinct: an explanation can appear convincing without faithfully identifying what influenced the prediction.

UNIREX treats rationale extraction as a learning problem with configurable components. Users choose an extractor architecture and objectives for faithfulness and plausibility, then jointly train the extractor and task model. This replaces heuristic design choices with a learned extractor that can be optimized alongside predictive performance. The authors also introduce Normalized Relative Gain, or NRG, to compare methods across the desired properties.

On five English text-classification datasets, the best UNIREX configuration exceeds the baselines by an average of 32.9% NRG. This is a gain in the proposed comparison metric, not a stated increase of that size in classification accuracy. The authors further find that extractor faithfulness can transfer to unseen datasets and tasks, suggesting that learned explanation behavior can extend beyond its training setting.
icml-2022-unirex-a-unified-learning-fram.tldr: UNIREX jointly learns predictions and text rationales to balance faithfulness, human plausibility, and task performance.

paragraphs: YourTTS applies multilingual training to speech synthesis for speakers beyond those represented during training. It builds on VITS with modifications supporting zero-shot multi-speaker and multilingual use. The work also addresses zero-shot voice conversion, extending its scope beyond generating speech from text.

The authors report state-of-the-art zero-shot multi-speaker synthesis and voice-conversion results comparable to the state of the art on VCTK. They also obtain promising results in a target language whose available dataset contains only one speaker. This suggests possibilities for extending multi-speaker synthesis and voice conversion to languages with limited speech resources.

A separate adaptation result shows that YourTTS can be fine-tuned using less than one minute of speech, achieving state-of-the-art voice similarity with reasonable quality. This matters for speakers whose voices or recording conditions differ substantially from the training data. The paper therefore presents both zero-shot capabilities and a small-data fine-tuning option; the latter’s reported similarity result involves adaptation and should not be read as a zero-shot result.
icml-2022-yourtts-towards-zero-shot-mult.tldr: YourTTS combines multilingual zero-shot speech synthesis and voice conversion with effective speaker adaptation from less than a minute of speech.
